# Every discontinuity in this engine, and which ones are the law

<!-- Generated by tools/cliffs/find-cliffs.mjs. Do not edit by hand. -->

A state income tax ought to be **continuous** in income: a cent more of wages
should never cost more than a cent of tax. Where it does, the law has a *notch*
and a filer has a reason to turn down a raise. Some of those notches are real —
written into a statute, printed on a form, and owed. Others are defects.

This file is the complete list for this engine, found by walking the tax function
itself rather than by sampling households.

```text
  household shapes swept        6
  states x years               42 x 2
  income points evaluated      938,448
  second-difference threshold   $3.00   (a flag, not a finding)
  smallest reported jump        $0.50

  DISCONTINUITIES FOUND        1569  (1085 distinct state-year-income notches)
    declared as a step         1563   a note names the provision AND says it steps
    named, not as a step       0   a note names it; nothing says it is a notch
    not named at all           0
    unattributable             6   the notch is in the rate schedule; no provision moved
  states with none             25 of 42
  sweep wall clock             163s
```

## How to read the four numbers, because none of them is an arithmetic defect

Every notch below is a figure this engine computes **from a table it transcribed
out of a statute or a form**. None of the four columns is an arithmetic error.
What they measure is what the package *tells a caller* about the shape of the
provision, which this repository treats as the same kind of obligation as the
figure itself: a provision that can cost a filer a hundred dollars on one cent of
income has a shape worth a sentence, and a caller who reads the notes and sees no
sentence will build a taper.

- **declared** — a note names the provision and says it steps, or quotes the
  step’s own dollar figure. Ohio’s `$18.69`, New York’s `$16.50` per `$1,000`,
  Connecticut’s four overlapping staircases, Missouri’s *"cliff chart and not a
  phase-out"*. Nothing is owed here.
- **named, not as a step** — a note names the provision and never says it is a
  notch. This is the queue, and it is a disclosure defect rather than a
  computation one.
- **not named at all** — no note mentions the provision. Rarer and worse.
- **unattributable** — the notch is in the rate schedule itself, so nothing in
  the result object names a provision and the classifier has no label to match.
  These need a reader. The state’s own notes about discontinuities are printed
  beside them.

### What `named` does NOT mean, measured on Day 77

The test is applied to ONE note at a time: a single string has to carry both the
provision’s name and a word from the step vocabulary. The notes are written as a
sequence of paragraphs, so a disclosure can be complete and still fail it. All six
groups this column held on Day 76 were read by hand, and **three of the six were
already disclosed:**

- Illinois said *"not phased out — it is lost entirely at the first dollar"* and priced
  the step, and no word in the vocabulary appears in that sentence.
- Arkansas named the Low Income Tax Tables in one note and called them staircases in
  the note two below, which began *"THE TABLES ARE STAIRCASES TOO"*.
- New York’s Empire State child credit declares its `$16.50` staircase in four
  sentences, every one of which refers to the credit as *"Its"* or *"The phase-out"*.

All three were reworded so that each note stands alone, which is what this package
claims of its notes anyway, and all three now pass. **The failure direction is the
expensive one:** this column over-reports. A reader who checks a row and finds that the
package already says it is reading correctly — it is the instrument that is wrong. Read
the note quoted under each group rather than trusting the count.

**Both queues are empty.**

## Found, but the result object names no provision

### AR 2026, childless-single — $10.00 at $97,270.00 of wages

```text
  wages $97,270.00 -> $97,270.01   total tax moves +$10.00
  stateAdjustedGrossIncome: 97270 -> 97270.01
  taxableIncome: 94800 -> 94800.01
  taxBeforeCredits: 3137.7 -> 3147.7
  tax: 3108.7 -> 3118.7
```

> PROVISIONAL, and the division is unusually clean: every RATE figure for 2026 is published law and every INDEXED figure is carried forward from 2025. Act 1 of the 2026 First Extraordinary Session prints the graduated schedule (0%, 2%, 3%, 3.4%, 3.7% at $5,600, $11,200, $16,000 and $26,400), the high-income table (2% on the first $4,700 and 3.7% above, on the whole net income) and all thirty rows of the bracket adjustment, so nothing on the rate side is a guess. What has not been published is the standard deduction, which § 26-51-430 indexes to CPI-U rounded DOWN to $10, the seven Low Income Tax Tables and their exempt amounts, which § 26-51-301 indexes, and the $26,500 threshold of the additional tax credit. The deduction exposure is the smallest in this package — one indexation step is $60 to $80 of deduction and $2.22 to $2.96 of tax — and the low-income tables are the larger one, in the other direction: an unindexed table charges a 2026 household whose income rose with inflation more rows than the real table will, so an Arkansas answer here is TOO HIGH for a low-income 2026 return by up to about $60.

> ARKANSAS'S HIGHEST MARGINAL RATE IS 13.70%, AND IT IS NOT IN ARKANSAS'S RATE SCHEDULE. A.C.A. § 26-51-201 has TWO schedules selected by income: a filer whose net taxable income does not exceed $94,700 pays the graduated table, and a filer one dollar above it pays 2% on the first $4,700 plus the top rate on every dollar above that, applied to their WHOLE net income, less a bracket adjustment of $290 that falls by $10 for each further $100 of income. A $10 relief withdrawn per $100 earned is ten percentage points of marginal rate, so the band from $94,701 to $97,600 is taxed at 13.70% in 2026 and the 2025 band from $94,701 to $97,800 at 13.90% — against top statutory rates of 3.7% and 3.9%. Nothing in any published Arkansas bracket table contains either figure.

## What the sweep cannot see

- **A notch inside a credit-absorbed region.** The sweep measures `totalTax`,
  which is floored at zero, so a notch where a credit already covers the whole
  bill moves nothing. Ohio’s `$342` constant is invisible to every shape here
  with children, because Ohio’s earned income credit covers the bill there.
- **A notch in a variable other than wages.** Investment income, municipal
  interest, itemised deductions and property tax are held at zero. A provision
  tested on one of those has its notch on that axis.
- **A notch smaller than the step can separate from a kink** — about `$3` below
  $150,000.00 of wages and about $50.00 above it, where the grid steps by $2,500.00.
- **Local income tax.** No county, city or school district is supplied, so
  Maryland and Indiana figures here are the state tax alone.

> Matched on `500`: THE STANDARD DEDUCTION IS A STAIRCASE THAT ROUNDS DOWN. § 40-18-15(b) reduces it by $25 for each $500 of Alabama AGI above $25,500 for a single filer — $175 per $500 joint, $135 per $500 head of family, $88 per $250 separate — to a floor of $2,500 ($5,000 joint). There is no "or fraction thereof" clause, so the first $499 above the threshold cost nothing and the step arrives on the five-hundredth dollar. Connecticut has the clause and charges the whole step on the first dollar: the two conventions are a step of deduction apart at every boundary of either chart.

> Matched on `94,700`: ARKANSAS'S HIGHEST MARGINAL RATE IS 13.70%, AND IT IS NOT IN ARKANSAS'S RATE SCHEDULE. A.C.A. § 26-51-201 has TWO schedules selected by income: a filer whose net taxable income does not exceed $94,700 pays the graduated table, and a filer one dollar above it pays 2% on the first $4,700 plus the top rate on every dollar above that, applied to their WHOLE net income, less a bracket adjustment of $290 that falls by $10 for each further $100 of income. A $10 relief withdrawn per $100 earned is ten percentage points of marginal rate, so the band from $94,701 to $97,600 is taxed at 13.70% in 2026 and the 2025 band from $94,701 to $97,800 at 13.90% — against top statutory rates of 3.7% and 3.9%. Nothing in any published Arkansas bracket table contains either figure.

> Matched on `140`: Connecticut's rate schedule scales exactly between filing statuses — single and separate are half the joint figures, head of household four fifths — and so does the tax recapture, except that a head of household's MIDDLE tier is $140 per $8,000 to a maximum of $4,200 where four fifths would be $144 and $4,320. The personal exemption, the add-back thresholds and the personal tax credit do not scale at all, and the single-filer figures a scaling model produces ($12,000 of exemption, a $50,250 add-back threshold) are real Connecticut numbers belonging to a SEPARATE filer. The error therefore survives a plausibility check.

> Matched on `24,000`: THE LOW-INCOME EXEMPTION IS DEAD FOR EVERY NON-ELDERLY IOWAN AND FOR EVERY JOINT RETURN, AND THE REASON IS ARITHMETIC RATHER THAN POLICY. § 422.5(3)'s four thresholds — $9,000, $13,500, $24,000, $32,000 — have not moved since at least 2021 and nothing indexes them. The test is on Iowa net income, BEFORE the deduction. So where a filer's own deduction already exceeds the threshold, a return at the threshold has no taxable income anyway and the exemption changes nothing: that is true of all five filing statuses under 65 in both 2025 and 2026, and of joint and surviving-spouse returns at 65 too. It still bites for a single, head-of-household or married-filing-separately filer aged 65 or over.

> Matched on `250,000`: Illinois' exemption allowance is a CLIFF and not a phase-out: 35 ILCS 5/204(g) disallows it entirely above $250,000 of federal AGI ($500,000 on a joint return), so one cent of extra income at the threshold costs a filer the whole allowance at once. For a single filer with no dependents that is $2,850 of exemption and $141.07 of tax in 2025, and $2,925 and $144.79 in 2026. THE $1,000 ADDITIONS FOR AGE AND BLINDNESS RIDE THE SAME CLIFF, so a single filer of 65 loses $3,850 of allowance and $190.57 of tax in 2025 ($3,925 and $194.29 in 2026). This note read $141.12 for the basic case until Day 77, which is 4.95% of $2,851 rather than of $2,850.

> Matched on `500`: Indiana's $1,000 exemption is the SMALLEST of the four on Schedule 3 and the only one a household total can find. On top of it: $1,500 more for each dependent CHILD — under 19, or under 24 and a full-time student — $1,000 for each filer at 65, $1,000 for each blind filer, and $500 MORE for each filer at 65 whose federal AGI is under $40,000 ($20,000 filing separately). All four are computed here from v0.21.0; before that a family with two children was $149.10 too high in Marion County and a retired couple under $40,000 was $149.10 too high as well.

> Matched on `15,650`: THE FAMILY SIZE TAX CREDIT (KRS 141.066, Schedule ITC Section C) is computed here from v0.62.0 and not before, and it was the largest gap in any state this package ships because it is a percentage of the WHOLE TAX. At or below a threshold amount set at the federal poverty guideline for the family size — $15,650, $21,150, $26,650 and $32,150 for sizes one to four in 2025 — it forgives 100% of the Kentucky tax, and it steps down to nothing at 133% of that figure. Until v0.62.0 a single Kentucky filer at exactly $15,650 was charged $495.20, which was the entire bill, and one at $8,000 was charged $189.20. The maximum family size is four (KRS 141.066(1)(e)4), so a fifth person moves nothing, and the credit applies to the tax REMAINING AFTER the $40 personal credits rather than to the tax before them — taking the percentage first would produce a negative tax on a credit that is not refundable.

> Matched on `maryland earned income credit / earned income credit / maryland poverty level credit / poverty level credit`: Maryland's earned income credit is ONE credit, not the two it is published as. The non-refundable half is 50% of the federal credit capped at the Maryland tax; the refundable half pays 45% of the federal credit less that tax. So the total is 45% of the federal credit for a filer with no tax and 50% for a filer with enough — an effective match that RISES with income across that band — and adding the two published percentages to get 95% is wrong by roughly the whole state tax.

> Matched on `subtraction`: Minnesota is one of the few states that taxes Social Security benefits at all. Since 2023 it subtracts the WHOLE federally taxable benefit below a threshold on federal AGI and withdraws the subtraction 10% for each $4,000 above it or fraction thereof — so it is gone once federal AGI exceeds the threshold by $36,000 ($18,000 on a separate return) and not by the $40,000 that ten steps of $4,000 suggests, for the same reason as the exemption staircase. This package models that simplified subtraction, § 290.0132, subd. 26(c).

> Matched on `50,000`: MISSOURI DEDUCTS A SHARE OF THE FEDERAL BILL AND THE CHART IS A CLIFF. § 143.171.2 gives 35% of the federal income tax at $25,000 or less of MISSOURI adjusted gross income, 25% to $50,000, 15% to $100,000, 5% to $125,000 and nothing above — one percentage for the whole bill, chosen by one number. So one dollar of income at a boundary moves the entire deduction down a step: at $100,000 the deduction falls by 10% of a federal bill of about $13,000, which is $61.94 OF MISSOURI TAX ON ONE DOLLAR. Pass `federal.incomeTaxBeforeRefundableCredits` — Form 1040 line 22 plus the Form 8960 net investment income tax. Omitting it makes the Missouri answer too HIGH by the whole deduction.

> Matched on `126`: Below the filing threshold — $10,000 of New Jersey gross income for a single or separate filer, $20,000 for every other status — there is no New Jersey tax at all, whatever the exemptions. One dollar above it the whole first bracket applies at once, so the threshold is a cliff whose size depends on the filer standing on it: about $126 for a single filer with one exemption and about $252 for a joint couple with two.

> Matched on `1,000`: THE AGED-OR-BLIND EXEMPTION HAS NOT BEEN INDEXED SINCE 1987 AND IT IS NINE CLIFFS, NOT A TAPER. § 7-2-5.2 gives up to $8,000 to each person 65 or over or blind, falling in whole $1,000 steps: single $8,000 to $18,000 of AGI then a step every $1,500 and nothing from $28,500; joint and head of household $8,000 to $30,000 then every $3,000 and nothing from $51,000; separate $8,000 to $15,000 then every $1,500 and nothing from $25,500. One dollar of AGI at a boundary costs the whole $1,000 of allowance AND MOST OF THE STEPS ARE STILL FREE: measured for 2026, four of the eight single boundaries cost nothing and the other four cost $14.27, $15.01, $30.34 and $32.04, because the exemption expires at $28,500 of AGI and a single New Mexican there has $8,125 of taxable income — inside the 3.2% band, so nobody who reaches 4.3% still holds the exemption. The largest step in the state is $64.04, at the joint $51,000 boundary, where both people's exemptions fall on the same dollar. Pricing these steps at the state's top rates is the mistake the first draft of this module made, and the measurement is what caught it. The thresholds are the 1987 figures on the reference model's parameter files, which carry every one of them from 1987-01-01 with no later value; the separate table is NOT half the joint one, unlike the rate schedule.

> Matched on `25,000`: THE HOUSEHOLD CREDIT IS A STEP CHART AND NOT A TAPER. Tax Law § 606(b) gives a flat amount per income ROW of New York adjusted gross income, so the credit does not slide — the dollar that crosses a row boundary costs the whole difference between the two rows at once. A single filer goes $75 / $60 / $50 / $45 / $40 / $20 / nothing, stepping at $5,000, $6,000, $7,000, $20,000, $25,000 and $28,000. Every other filing status starts from $90 / $75 / $65 / $60 / $50 / $40 / $20 / nothing, stepping at $5,000, $6,000, $7,000, $22,000, $25,000, $28,000 and $32,000, and adds for each household member after the first an amount that steps on its own: $15 / $10 / $5 / nothing at $20,000, $25,000 and $32,000. So the steps run $5 to $25 for a one- or two-person household and grow with household size. It is the same shape as the Empire State child credit's $16.50 staircase and it is written into the same section, but no table prints it as a percentage of anything, so a caller who reads the credit as a phase-out of the $90 will be wrong at every boundary.

> Matched on `0.01`: Ohio's rate schedule is DISCONTINUOUS and this is not a rounding artifact. O.R.C. § 5747.02(A)(3) charges a flat constant the moment Ohio taxable nonbusiness income clears $26,050 — $342.00 for 2025, $332.00 from 2026 — on top of 2.75% of the excess. A filer at $26,050 owes $0 and a filer at $26,050.01 owes $342.00. Reading the printed table as ordinary marginal brackets, which is what "Ohio: 0% / 2.75% / 3.125%" invites, understates every Ohio filer above the threshold by the whole constant.

> Matched on `256`: Not modelled, and each is a credit rather than a rate: the Working Family Household and Dependent Care credit (ORS 315.264, a percentage of care expenses that falls with income and is the largest credit on many working parents' returns); the additional exemption credit for a filer with a severe disability and the one for a dependent child with a disability (ORS 316.099, both an extra exemption at $256/$263 and the second with an income limit of its own); the 529/ABLE contribution credit (ORS 315.650); and the political contribution credit. Pass any of these through as credits you compute yourself. The Oregon surplus "kicker" is NO LONGER on this list — it is modelled, and needs `oregonPriorYearTaxBeforeCredits`.

> Matched on `special tax forgiveness`: Special Tax Forgiveness is a staircase, not a phase-out: full forgiveness up to the allowance, then ten percentage points less for each $250 of eligibility income above it, reaching zero $2,500 later. Because each step forgives ten points less of the WHOLE tax, the cost of a step grows with the household. Across the band a single filer faces about 11% and a single parent of two about 34%, against a statutory 3.07%.

> Matched on `11,950`: Below the filing threshold Virginia charges nothing at all: $11,950 of Virginia AGI for every status but joint, $23,900 joint (§ 58.1-321). It is a cliff, and it has not moved since 2021 while the standard deduction nearly doubled, so it now sits above the point where tax would otherwise begin.
